plan.title: Grade 3 Bible & Christian Studies — Course Plan

sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The outline describes this course as a chronological Bible survey, Scripture memory, catechism, hymn study and church history, running alongside the history cycle so that biblical events are placed on the same timeline as the rest of history (§3F). It opens the daily core with ten minutes every day (§7).

Grade 3 reads the whole Bible story in order, from Creation to the early Church, in one year, at a level a Grade 3 child can carry. It also memorizes a passage of Scripture each term, learns the three classic parts of Christian teaching (the Nicene Creed, the Commandments and the Lord's Prayer), sings a hymn each term, and hears the church history of the Colonial period that History & Geography is studying.
Scripture is read as written, and the course stays with what the historic churches hold in common. Families are encouraged to add their own church's catechism and practices.

blocks.text: Translations:
Old Testament: the Septuagint, the ancient Greek Old Testament, in Sir Lancelot Brenton's English translation (1844, public domain). The term manuals print the Old Testament passages from Brenton.
New Testament: the World English Bible (public domain, modern English). The term manuals print the New Testament passages from it.
Brenton's English is older in style ("thou", "hast"). It's printed as Brenton wrote it.

Psalm numbers: the Septuagint numbers most psalms one lower than the Hebrew-based Bibles most families own. The manuals give the Septuagint number first and the Hebrew number in brackets: Psalm 22 [23]. Brenton also counts a psalm's title as verse 1, so verse numbers can differ by one as well.
Each term's passage is also Penmanship's Scripture copywork (course 04) and goes into the Memory Work queue (course 11), so the daily core works on it three ways.
The three classic parts of Christian teaching, common to the historic churches, taught by simple question and answer on Day 4:

blocks.text: A family whose church has its own catechism may use it on Day 4 instead, or alongside.

blocks.text: Bible is a course of formation as well as knowledge, so it isn't graded.
Narration (Day 2): oral, every week.

Bible story order check (week 6 of each term): the child puts the term's six stories in order on the timeline. Not scored; any confusion is reviewed.

Year-end: the child retells the whole Bible story, from Creation to Pentecost, in a few minutes, using the timeline pages; and recites the year's six passages, the Nicene Creed, the Commandments and the Lord's Prayer.

blocks.text: Bible is daily, but each lesson is short. If days are missed, pick up at the next lesson; don't double up.
A missed Bible story can be read at any time, but keep the stories in order. The point of the survey is the sequence.
Scripture memory and the hymn carry over until they're known; there's no rush to start the next term's passage.

sections.title: 11. What each term manual will contain

blocks.text: For each week: the Bible passage reference and a narration prompt, the timeline entry, the memory lines for that week, the catechism question and answer, and the hymn or church-history story. For each term: the full Scripture passage, the full hymn text, and the story-order check.

head: Bible survey
Creation · the Fall · Noah and Babel · Abraham · Isaac and Jacob · Joseph (Genesis)
rows: The Nicene Creed, first part: lines 1–5, from "We believe in one God" to "he suffered death and was buried"
"Praise God, from Whom All Blessings Flow" (the Doxology), Thomas Ken, 1674
The Pilgrims · the Puritans · the Bay Psalm Book
5 a week, about 10 minutes each: Day 1 Read · Day 2 Narrate · Day 3 Memory · Day 4 Catechism · Day 5 Hymn or church history

glance.text: Reading the Old Testament. The parent reads each week's passage from Brenton's English Septuagint (public domain, free online). Genesis has the same chapter numbers in Brenton as in other Bibles. A long chapter can be shortened to the verses that tell the story; 10–20 verses is enough at this age.
Bible opens the daily core, so it's usually the first ten minutes of the school day.

blocks.text: Brenton's Septuagint. The first line in Brenton is the title, "A Psalm of David."
1 The Lord tends me as a shepherd, and I shall want nothing.
2 In a place of green grass, there he has made me dwell: he has nourished me by the water of rest.
3 He has restored my soul: he has guided me into the paths of righteousness, for his name's sake.
4 Yea, even if I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will not be afraid of evils: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff, these have comforted me.
5 Thou hast prepared a table before me in presence of them that afflict me: thou hast thoroughly anointed my head with oil; and thy cup cheers me like the best wine.
6 Thy mercy also shall follow me all the days of my life: and my dwelling shall be in the house of the Lord for a very long time.
Words to explain: tends (looks after) · want (lack, be without) · nourished (fed) · righteousness (what is right) · thou, thy (you, your) · afflict (trouble) · anointed (poured oil on, as an honor).
This is also Penmanship's Scripture copywork this term, and it goes into the Memory Work queue.
Praise God, from whom all blessings flow;
Praise Him, all creatures here below;
Praise Him above, ye heavenly host;
Praise Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Amen.
Thomas Ken, 1674. Sung to the tune "Old Hundredth".

The Nicene Creed in the common modern English wording (English Language Liturgical Consultation, 1988), with the line on the Holy Spirit as the Council of Constantinople wrote it in 381. A family whose church uses the Apostles' Creed may learn that instead.
1 We believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all that is, seen and unseen.
2 We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, eternally begotten of the Father,
3 God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one Being with the Father; through him all things were made.
4 For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary and became truly human.
5 For our sake he was crucified under Pontius Pilate; he suffered death and was buried.
(Term 2 continues with lines 6–10, from "On the third day he rose again".)
Genesis 1:1–2:3: the six days of creation and the seventh day of rest.
"What did God make on each day?" Timeline: start the Bible pages with Creation, and draw the seven days as seven small boxes.
Psalm 22, verse 1.
Q: Who made heaven and earth? A: God, the Father, the Almighty. Learn line 1 of the Creed.
Learn the Doxology, the first two lines.
Genesis 3: the serpent, the fruit and the garden left behind; then Genesis 4:1–16: Cain and Abel.
"Why did Adam and Eve have to leave the garden?" Timeline: the Fall.
Psalm 22, verse 2; review verse 1.
Q: Who is Jesus Christ? A: The only Son of God. Learn line 2 of the Creed.

The Pilgrims: they crossed the ocean in 1620 so they could worship God as they believed was right, and on the Mayflower they read the Bible and sang psalms. (Literature and History meet the Pilgrims this term too.) Then sing the Doxology.

weeks.title: Noah and the tower of Babel

blocks.text: Genesis 6:9–9:17, shortened: Noah builds the ark, the flood, the rainbow and God's promise.
"What promise did God make with the rainbow?" Timeline: the Flood. Also read Genesis 11:1–9, the tower of Babel, and add Babel.
Psalm 22, verse 3; review verses 1–2.
Q: Through whom were all things made? A: Through the Son. Learn line 3 of the Creed.
The Doxology, all four lines.
Genesis 12:1–8: God calls Abram to leave his home; then Genesis 15:1–6: the promise of descendants as many as the stars.
"What did God promise Abraham?" Timeline: Abraham. Draw a night sky full of stars.
Psalm 22, verse 4; review verses 1–3.
Q: Why did the Son come down from heaven? A: For us and for our salvation. Learn line 4 of the Creed.

The Puritans came to Massachusetts Bay in 1630 to build a community ordered by their faith. Their leader, John Winthrop, hoped it would be like "a city upon a hill" (Matthew 5:14). Then sing the Doxology.
Genesis 25:19–34: the twins Jacob and Esau; then Genesis 28:10–22: Jacob's dream of the ladder to heaven.
"What did Jacob see in his dream?" Timeline: Isaac and Jacob.
Psalm 22, verses 5–6; review verses 1–4.
Q: What did Jesus suffer for us? A: He was crucified under Pontius Pilate; he suffered death and was buried. Learn line 5 of the Creed.
The Doxology; the child leads the family in singing it.

intro.text: Story-order check (week 6, Day 2)
The parent reads these in jumbled order: Joseph in Egypt · the Flood · Creation · Abraham · Jacob's dream · the Fall · the tower of Babel.
Correct order: Creation · the Fall · the Flood · the tower of Babel · Abraham · Jacob's dream · Joseph in Egypt.
Not scored. If the order is shaky, read back through the timeline pages together.

blocks.text: Joseph: Genesis 37 (the coat and the brothers), shortened; then the end of the story in Genesis 45:1–15, when Joseph forgives his brothers. (Read chapters 39–44 aloud at another time if the family wants the whole story.)
"How did Joseph treat his brothers at the end?" Timeline: Joseph in Egypt. Then the story-order check (below).
Recite Psalm 22 from memory, all six verses.
Recite lines 1–5 of the Creed.

Term-end recitation before the family or co-op: Psalm 22, lines 1–5 of the Nicene Creed, and the Doxology sung. Church history: the Bay Psalm Book (1640), a book of psalms for singing, was the first book printed in English America.
Read the Bible itself. Brenton's English is old-fashioned; read it slowly, and stop to explain a word when needed. Children quickly get used to it, and it's the language of the memory passage too.
Ten minutes means ten minutes. If a reading runs long, shorten it. The story matters more than every verse.
The memory passage goes three ways: Bible (Day 3), Penmanship (copywork) and Memory Work (daily recitation). Coordinate so the child is copying and reciting the same verse each week.
Find Brenton's Septuagint online or in print, and bookmark Genesis
Print Psalm 22, the Creed lines and the Doxology (or the Apostles' Creed, if the family uses it)
Give the week's Psalm verse to Penmanship and Memory Work
Week 6: hold the recitation and do the story-order check

William Penn and the Quakers · John Eliot's Bible
5 a week, about 10 minutes each: Day 1 Read · Day 2 Narrate · Day 3 Memory · Day 4 Catechism · Day 5 Hymn or church history

glance.text: Reading the Old Testament. Read from Brenton's English Septuagint. Exodus, Joshua, Judges and Ruth have the same chapter numbers as in other Bibles. Shorten long chapters to the verses that tell the story.

blocks.text: Brenton's Septuagint. Brenton's verse 1 begins with the title, "A Psalm for Thanksgiving."
1 Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth.
2 Serve the Lord with gladness; come before his presence with exultation.
3 Know that the Lord he is God; he made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
4 Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with hymns; give thanks to him, praise his name.
5 For the Lord is good, his mercy is for ever; and his truth endures to generation and generation.
Words to explain: exultation (great joy) · pasture (a field where sheep graze) · courts (the open yards of the temple).

reference.title: The hymn: "All People That on Earth Do Dwell"

blocks.text: William Kethe, 1561: Psalm 100 set as a hymn, sung to "Old Hundredth", the same tune as Term 1's Doxology. Wording varies a little between hymnals; use your church's version if it differs.
All people that on earth do dwell,
Sing to the Lord with cheerful voice;
Him serve with mirth, his praise forth tell,
Come ye before him and rejoice.
The Lord, ye know, is God indeed;
Without our aid he did us make;
We are his folk, he doth us feed,
And for his sheep he doth us take.
Point out that the hymn and the memory psalm are the same psalm, one sung and one said.
6 On the third day he rose again in accordance with the Scriptures; he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.
7 He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.
8 We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, who has spoken through the prophets.
9 We believe in one holy catholic and apostolic Church. We acknowledge one baptism for the forgiveness of sins.
10 We look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come. Amen.
Line 8 is printed as the Council of Constantinople wrote it in 381. Many Western churches say "who proceeds from the Father and the Son"; use your church's wording.
Exodus 2:1–10: baby Moses in the basket on the river; then Exodus 3:1–12: the bush that burned and was not burned up.
"What did God tell Moses from the bush?" Timeline: Moses.
Psalm 99, verse 1; review Psalm 22.
Review lines 1–5. Q: What happened on the third day? A: He rose again. Learn line 6.
Learn "All People That on Earth Do Dwell", the first four lines.
Exodus 7:14–24: the first plague (the river turned to blood); then Exodus 12:21–32: the Passover and Israel set free. Tell the other plagues briefly.
"What did the Israelites do on the night of the Passover?" Timeline: the Passover.
Psalm 99, verse 2; review verse 1.
Q: Will Jesus come again? A: Yes, in glory, to judge the living and the dead. Learn line 7.
William Penn and the Quakers: Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a place where people of many churches could worship freely. (History reads about Penn in week 9.) Then sing the hymn.

weeks.title: The Red Sea and the manna

blocks.text: Exodus 14:21–31: crossing the Red Sea; then Exodus 16:13–21: manna in the wilderness.
"How did God feed his people in the wilderness?" Timeline: the Red Sea.
Psalm 99, verse 3; review verses 1–2.
Q: Who is the giver of life? A: The Holy Spirit. Learn line 8.
The hymn, all eight lines.
Exodus 19:16–20: God comes down on Mount Sinai in thunder and smoke; then Exodus 20:1–17: the Ten Commandments.
"Where did God give the Ten Commandments, and what was the mountain like?" Timeline: Sinai. (The child memorizes the Commandments in Terms 3–4.)
Psalm 99, verse 4; review verses 1–3.
Q: What do we believe about the Church? A: We believe in one holy catholic and apostolic Church. Learn line 9.

John Eliot's Bible: in 1663 John Eliot, a minister in Massachusetts, published the whole Bible translated into the language of the Massachusett people, the first complete Bible printed in America. Then sing the hymn.
Joshua 1:1–9: "be strong and courageous"; then Joshua 6:1–20, shortened: the walls of Jericho.
"How did the walls of Jericho fall?" Timeline: Joshua and Jericho.
Psalm 99, verse 5; review verses 1–4.
Q: What do we look for? A: The resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come. Learn line 10.
The hymn; the child leads the family in singing it.

intro.text: Story-order check (week 12, Day 2)
The parent reads these in jumbled order: the Red Sea · Ruth · the burning bush · Jericho · the Passover · Mount Sinai.
Correct order: the burning bush · the Passover · the Red Sea · Mount Sinai · Jericho · Ruth.
Not scored. If the order is shaky, read back through the timeline pages together.

blocks.text: Judges 7:1–8, 16–21, shortened: Gideon's 300 men with trumpets and torches; then Ruth 1:1–18: Ruth stays with Naomi ("thy people shall be my people").
"What did Ruth promise Naomi?" Timeline: the Judges and Ruth. Then the story-order check (below).
Recite Psalm 99 from memory; then Psalm 22 again.
Recite the whole Nicene Creed, lines 1–10.
Term-end recitation before the family or co-op: Psalm 99, the Nicene Creed, and the hymn sung.
The whole Creed by week 12. Ten lines in twelve weeks is a lot. If line 8 or 9 isn't secure, carry it into Term 3's Day 4 alongside the Commandments.
Same psalm, two ways. Psalm 99 [100] is both this term's memory passage and its hymn. Children love discovering that.
Keep it ten minutes. Exodus is full of long chapters; read the story, not every verse.
Print Psalm 99, Creed lines 6–10, and the hymn
Give the week's Psalm verse to Penmanship and Memory Work
Week 12: hold the recitation and do the story-order check

head: Bible survey
Samuel · David anointed · David and Goliath · King David and the Psalms · Solomon and the temple · Elijah
rows: Luke 2:8–14, World English Bible (the Christmas season)
The Ten Commandments, 1–5, from Brenton's Exodus 20
The Great Awakening: George Whitefield · Jonathan Edwards
5 a week, about 10 minutes each: Day 1 Read · Day 2 Narrate · Day 3 Memory · Day 4 Catechism · Day 5 Hymn or church history

glance.text: Book names in Brenton. The Septuagint calls the books of Samuel and Kings Kings I–IV. Kings I is 1 Samuel, Kings II is 2 Samuel, Kings III is 1 Kings, and Kings IV is 2 Kings. The readings below give Brenton's name first and the usual name in brackets. Chapter numbers are the same.
Christmas. This term falls across Christmas. The memory passage is the angels' announcement to the shepherds, from the New Testament, ahead of Term 5's life of Jesus.

blocks.text: World English Bible.
8 There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock.
9 Behold, an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
10 The angel said to them, "Don't be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people.
11 For there is born to you today, in David's city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
12 This is the sign to you: you will find a baby wrapped in strips of cloth, lying in a feeding trough."
13 Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God and saying,
14 "Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men."
Words to explain: Christ (the Anointed One) · feeding trough (a manger, where animals eat) · multitude (a great crowd).
Link to this term's story: "David's city" is Bethlehem, where David was born. The child meets David in weeks 14–16.
Isaac Watts, 1719.
Joy to the world! the Lord is come;
Let earth receive her King;
Let every heart prepare him room,
And heaven and nature sing.
Joy to the earth! the Saviour reigns;
Let men their songs employ;
While fields and floods, rocks, hills, and plains
Repeat the sounding joy.
From Brenton's Septuagint, Exodus 20, in short form.
1 Thou shalt have no other gods beside me.
2 Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol.
3 Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain.
4 Remember the sabbath day to keep it holy.
5 Honour thy father and thy mother.

Churches number the Commandments in different ways. This is the numbering of the early Church and of the Orthodox and many Protestant churches. A family whose church numbers them differently should use its own numbering.
Kings I 3:1–10 [1 Samuel 3]: the boy Samuel hears God calling in the night.
"What did Samuel say when God called him the third time?" Timeline: Samuel.
Luke 2, verses 8–9.
Q: What is the first commandment? A: Thou shalt have no other gods beside me.
Learn "Joy to the World", the first stanza.
Kings I 16:1–13 [1 Samuel 16]: Samuel anoints the shepherd boy David, the youngest of his brothers.
"Why did Samuel choose David, the youngest?" Timeline: David anointed.
Luke 2, verse 10; review 8–9.
Q: What is the second commandment? A: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol.

George Whitefield crossed from England to the American colonies several times from 1739 and preached outdoors to crowds of thousands. Benjamin Franklin heard him in Philadelphia and wrote about how far his voice carried. (Literature read about Franklin in Term 2.) Then sing the hymn.
Kings I 17:32–50 [1 Samuel 17], shortened: David faces Goliath with a sling and five stones.
"What did David take with him to meet Goliath?" Timeline: David and Goliath.
Luke 2, verse 11; review 8–10.
Q: What is the third commandment? A: Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain.
"Joy to the World", both stanzas.
Kings II 5:1–5 [2 Samuel 5]: David becomes king over all Israel; then Kings II 6:12–15 [2 Samuel 6]: David brings the ark to Jerusalem with music and dancing.

"What city did David make his capital?" Timeline: King David, about 1000 BC, the first dated event on the Bible pages. Remind the child that David wrote many of the Psalms, including Psalm 22 [23] from Term 1.
Luke 2, verse 12; review 8–11.
Q: What is the fourth commandment? A: Remember the sabbath day to keep it holy.
Jonathan Edwards, a minister in Northampton, Massachusetts, was a leader of the Great Awakening in the 1730s and 1740s, when many people in the colonies turned to faith. Then sing the hymn.
Kings III 3:5–14 [1 Kings 3]: Solomon asks God for wisdom; then Kings III 8:1–11 [1 Kings 8], shortened: the temple is finished and filled with God's glory.
"What did Solomon ask God for, and why?" Timeline: Solomon builds the temple.
Luke 2, verses 13–14; review 8–12.
Q: What is the fifth commandment? A: Honour thy father and thy mother.
"Joy to the World"; the child leads the singing.

intro.text: Story-order check (week 18, Day 2)
The parent reads these in jumbled order: David and Goliath · Elijah on Mount Carmel · the boy Samuel · Solomon's temple · David anointed · King David in Jerusalem.
Correct order: the boy Samuel · David anointed · David and Goliath · King David in Jerusalem · Solomon's temple · Elijah on Mount Carmel.
Not scored.

blocks.text: Kings III 18:20–39 [1 Kings 18], shortened: Elijah on Mount Carmel, and the fire from heaven.
"What happened on Mount Carmel?" Timeline: Elijah. Then the story-order check (below).
Recite Luke 2:8–14; then Psalms 22 and 99 again.
Recite Commandments 1–5; review the Nicene Creed.
Term-end recitation before the family or co-op: Luke 2:8–14, Commandments 1–5, and "Joy to the World" sung.
Two translations, two styles. The Old Testament readings are in Brenton's older English; the memory passage is in the modern World English Bible. Both are read as written.
Christmas fits naturally. If the family's Christmas break falls mid-term, keep the memory passage and the hymn going over the holiday. They suit the season.
The Commandments are short to memorize but worth talking about simply: what each one asks of us, in a sentence.
Note the Brenton book names (Kings I–IV) before week 13
Print Luke 2:8–14, Commandments 1–5, and "Joy to the World"
Give the week's verse to Penmanship and Memory Work
Week 18: hold the recitation and do the story-order check

glance.text: Book names in Brenton. Isaiah is titled Esaias and Jonah Jonas. Kings IV is 2 Kings. Brenton's Esther and Daniel are the Greek versions, which include some passages not found in other Bibles; the stories below are the same, but verse numbers may differ, so find the scene described.

blocks.text: Brenton's Septuagint. Verse 1 in Brenton is the title.
2 God is our refuge and strength, a help in the afflictions that have come heavily upon us.
3 Therefore will we not fear when the earth is troubled, and the mountains are removed into the depths of the seas.
4 Their waters have roared and been troubled, the mountains have been troubled by his might. Pause.
11 Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.
12 The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our helper.

Words to explain: refuge (a safe place to run to) · afflictions (troubles) · exalted (lifted up, honored) · hosts (armies, here the armies of heaven). "Pause" marks a rest in the psalm when it was sung.

reference.title: The hymn: "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God"

blocks.text: Martin Luther, 1529, based on this term's psalm; English by Frederic H. Hedge, 1853.
A mighty fortress is our God,
A bulwark never failing;
Our helper He amid the flood
Of mortal ills prevailing:
For still our ancient foe
Doth seek to work us woe;
His craft and power are great,
And, armed with cruel hate,
On earth is not his equal.
Words to explain: fortress, bulwark (a strong castle, a strong wall) · ancient foe (the devil) · woe (harm).
From Brenton's Septuagint, Exodus 20, in short form.
6 Thou shalt not commit adultery.
7 Thou shalt not steal.
8 Thou shalt not kill.
9 Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
10 Thou shalt not covet … whatever belongs to thy neighbour.
In the Septuagint, commandments 6–8 come in the order adultery, steal, kill. Most other Bibles have kill, adultery, steal. Families should use the order of their own Bible and church.
Kings IV 5:1–14 [2 Kings 5]: Naaman the army captain is told to wash seven times in the river Jordan.
"Why didn't Naaman want to wash in the Jordan at first?" Timeline: Elisha.
Psalm 45, verse 2; review the Christmas passage.
Review Commandments 1–5. Q: What is the sixth commandment? A: Thou shalt not commit adultery: keep the promises of marriage.
Learn "A Mighty Fortress", the first four lines.
Jonas [Jonah] 1–3, shortened: Jonah runs from God, the storm, the great fish, and Nineveh.
"Where did God send Jonah, and what did Jonah do instead?" Timeline: Jonah.
Psalm 45, verse 3; review verse 2.
Q: What is the seventh commandment? A: Thou shalt not steal.

Isaac Watts (1674–1748), an English pastor, wrote about 750 hymns, including Term 3's "Joy to the World" and next term's "O God, Our Help in Ages Past". His hymns were sung across the American colonies. Then sing the hymn.
Esaias [Isaiah] 9:6–7: the promise of a child to be born, whose kingdom will have no end. Read it as Brenton gives it. (The wording in the Septuagint differs from other Bibles here.)
"What did Isaiah promise would come?" Timeline: Isaiah. Point out the Creed's line "his kingdom will have no end" (line 7).
Psalm 45, verse 4; review verses 2–3.
Q: What is the eighth commandment? A: Thou shalt not kill.
"A Mighty Fortress", all nine lines.
Daniel 6, shortened: Daniel keeps praying to God, is thrown into the lions' den, and is kept safe.
"Why was Daniel put in the lions' den?" Timeline: the exile in Babylon, and Daniel.
Psalm 45, verse 11; review verses 2–4.
Q: What is the ninth commandment? A: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour: don't tell lies about others.

Charles Wesley (1707–1788), an English minister, wrote more than 6,000 hymns, including "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing". He and his brother John visited the colony of Georgia in the 1730s. (History reads about Georgia in Term 2.) Then sing the hymn.
Esther, Brenton's Greek version: the scenes where Esther agrees to go to the king to save her people, and the king holds out his golden sceptre to her (chapters 4–5; find the scene).
"What did Esther risk, and what happened?" Timeline: Esther.
Psalm 45, verse 12; review 2–4 and 11.
Q: What is the tenth commandment? A: Thou shalt not covet whatever belongs to thy neighbour: don't long for what is someone else's.
"A Mighty Fortress"; the child leads the singing.

The Septuagint shows its differences this term: the order of the Commandments, Isaiah's wording, and the longer Greek Esther and Daniel. They're printed and read as Brenton gives them.
The hymn and the psalm match again. Luther wrote "A Mighty Fortress" from this term's psalm.
By week 24 the child knows all Ten Commandments. Say them together often, at the table or before bed.

glance.text: Reading the New Testament. From this term the readings come from the World English Bible (public domain, modern English). The Gospels have the same chapter and verse numbers in every Bible.

blocks.text: World English Bible.
3 "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
4 Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
5 Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.

reference.title: The hymn: "O God, Our Help in Ages Past"

blocks.text: Isaac Watts, 1719, based on Psalm 89 [90]. First, second and last stanzas.
O God, our help in ages past,
Our hope for years to come,
Our shelter from the stormy blast,
And our eternal home.
Under the shadow of thy throne
Thy saints have dwelt secure;
Sufficient is thine arm alone,
And our defence is sure.
O God, our help in ages past,
Our hope for years to come,
Be thou our guard while life shall last,
And our eternal home.
Matthew 6:9–12, World English Bible.
Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come.
Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
A family that says the Lord's Prayer in its church's traditional wording ("Our Father, who art in heaven…") may use that instead.

Q: What do we pray for next? A: Let your Kingdom come.

The American Bible Society was founded in 1816 to print Bibles and send them across the growing country, so that families on the frontier could have one. (History follows the westward settlers this term.) Then sing the hymn.
Mark 4:35–41: Jesus calms the storm; then John 6:1–14: the feeding of the five thousand.
"What did the disciples say after Jesus calmed the storm?" Timeline: the miracles of Jesus.
Matthew 5, verse 6; review 3–5.

"Who was a good neighbor to the hurt man?" Timeline: the parables. Remind the child of Psalm 22 [23] from Term 1: another shepherd.
Matthew 5, verses 7–8; review 3–6.
Q: What do we ask God to give us? A: Give us today our daily bread.
Circuit riders were preachers who traveled on horseback from settlement to settlement on the frontier, leading worship wherever a few families gathered. Then sing the hymn.
Matthew 5:1–16: Jesus teaches on the mountain: the Beatitudes, and "you are the light of the world".
"Jesus said his followers are like salt and light. What did he mean?" Timeline: the Sermon on the Mount. The memory passage comes from this reading.
Matthew 5, verses 9–10; review 3–8.
Q: What do we ask about forgiveness? A: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
All three stanzas; the child leads the singing.

glance.text: Easter. This term reads the Crucifixion and the Resurrection. If Easter falls during Term 5 instead, swap the two terms' readings so the stories meet the season.

blocks.text: World English Bible.
4 Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn't envy. Love doesn't brag, is not proud,
5 doesn't behave itself inappropriately, doesn't seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
6 doesn't rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;
7 bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.
8 Love never fails.

Words to explain: envy (wish you had what someone else has) · brag (boast) · provoked (made angry) · takes no account of evil (doesn't keep a list of wrongs) · endures (keeps going through hard things).
John Newton, 1779. The first three stanzas, as he wrote them.
Amazing grace! (how sweet the sound)
That saved a wretch like me!
I once was lost, but now am found,
Was blind, but now I see.
'Twas grace that taught my heart to fear,
And grace my fears relieved;
How precious did that grace appear
The hour I first believed!
Through many dangers, toils and snares,
I have already come;
'Tis grace has brought me safe thus far,
And grace will lead me home.
Words to explain: grace (God's love and help, freely given) · wretch (a person in a miserable state) · snares (traps).
Matthew 6:13, World English Bible.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.
For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.
The last line is found in many ancient copies of Matthew and is said in many churches; some Bibles print it only in a note. Families use their church's practice.
Luke 23:33–46, shortened: Jesus is crucified; "Father, forgive them"; the thief on the cross; Jesus dies.
"What did Jesus say about the people who crucified him?" Timeline: the Crucifixion. Link to the Creed, line 5: "For our sake he was crucified under Pontius Pilate."
1 Corinthians 13, verse 4; review Matthew 5:3–10.
Review the first part of the Lord's Prayer. Q: What do we ask God to keep us from? A: Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.
Learn "Amazing Grace", the first stanza.
Luke 24:1–12: the women find the empty tomb, and the angels say "He isn't here, but is risen."
"What did the women find at the tomb?" Timeline: the Resurrection. Link to the Creed, line 6: "On the third day he rose again."
1 Corinthians 13, verse 5; review verse 4.
Q: How does the Lord's Prayer end? A: For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen. Say the whole prayer together.

John Newton (1725–1807) worked at sea for many years, including on ships in the slave trade. Later he became a pastor in Olney, England, and wrote "Amazing Grace" about God's grace in his own life. Then sing the hymn.
Acts 1:6–11: Jesus is taken up into heaven; then Acts 2:1–4: the Holy Spirit comes at Pentecost.
"What happened on the day of Pentecost?" Timeline: the Ascension and Pentecost. Link to the Creed, lines 6 and 8.
1 Corinthians 13, verse 6; review 4–5.
The whole Lord's Prayer, said from memory.
"Amazing Grace", the first two stanzas.
Acts 2:42–47: the first believers share everything and meet together; then Acts 3:1–10: Peter heals the man at the temple gate.
"What did Peter say to the man who asked for money?" Timeline: the first Church.
1 Corinthians 13, verse 7; review 4–6.
Review the Ten Commandments, all ten.
Sunday schools: in 1780 Robert Raikes, in Gloucester, England, started schools on Sundays to teach poor children to read, using the Bible. Sunday schools soon spread to America. Then sing the hymn.

Acts 9:1–19: Saul meets Jesus on the road to Damascus and becomes Paul. Then tell briefly how Paul traveled to many cities, starting churches and writing letters, including the letter to Corinth that holds this term's memory passage.
"What happened to Saul on the road to Damascus?" Timeline: Paul. Find Damascus, Jerusalem, Corinth and Rome on a map.
1 Corinthians 13, verse 8a; review 4–7.
Review the Nicene Creed, all ten lines.
"Amazing Grace", all three stanzas; the child leads the singing.
